subject: ent
title: Laryngeal Cartilages, Muscles and Nerve Supply

steps.tx: **Laryngeal cartilages** form the voice box skeleton: unpaired thyroid, cricoid and epiglottis with paired arytenoid, corniculate and cuneiform cartilages joined by membranes and moved by intrinsic muscles. The cricoid is the only complete ring in the airway and the narrowest point in a child. Thyroid cartilage shields the vocal folds and provides the surface landmarks by which the airway is found in emergencies.
steps.say: Thyroid, cricoid and epiglottic cartilages with three paired cartilages form the voice box skeleton. The cricoid ring is complete and gives the narrowest point in children. Surface landmarks guide emergency airway access reliably.

vis.alt: Diagram of laryngeal cartilages, intrinsic muscles and nerve supply of the larynx.
vis.caption: Laryngeal framework, muscles and nerves. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The **posterior cricoarytenoid** is the only abductor of the vocal cords, opening the glottis for breathing while every other intrinsic muscle adducts, tenses or relaxes the folds. Its solitary role explains why bilateral abductor failure obstructs the airway while unilateral failure mainly hoarsens voice. Examiners return to this muscle constantly because one fact predicts the presentation of every bilateral cord palsy.
steps.say: One muscle opens the cords for breathing while all others close or tense them. Bilateral failure causes airway obstruction and unilateral failure causes hoarseness mainly. Solitary abductor status explains cord palsy presentations completely.

steps.tx: **Intrinsic laryngeal muscles** receive motor supply from the recurrent laryngeal nerve except cricothyroid, which the external branch of superior laryngeal nerve supplies. Sensory supply divides at the cords: superior laryngeal internal branch above, recurrent nerve below. This split predicts injury patterns in thyroid surgery, where external branch damage flattens pitch range while recurrent damage paralyses cord movement itself.
steps.say: Recurrent nerves supply all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid tensor muscle. Sensory supply divides at cord level between superior and recurrent branches. Thyroid surgery injuries separate pitch loss from movement loss accordingly.

steps.tx: The **recurrent laryngeal nerve** loops under the subclavian artery on the right and aortic arch on the left, ascending in the tracheo-oesophageal groove to enter the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint. Its long left course explains vulnerability to mediastinal tumours, aortic disease and thyroid surgery alike. Non recurrent right nerve with aberrant subclavian artery is the variant that traps unwary thyroid surgeons.
steps.say: Right nerve loops under subclavian artery while left nerve loops under the aortic arch. Long left course explains vulnerability to chest tumours and thyroid surgery. Aberrant right anatomy produces a non recurrent variant surgically.

steps.tx: The **superior laryngeal nerve** injury after thyroid surgery or carotid procedures leaves loss of high pitch and early vocal fatigue from cricothyroid weakness, with supraglottic sensory loss risking silent aspiration. Singers notice pitch injury first, which is why voice professionals need specific consent about the external branch. Recurrent injury instead gives breathy hoarseness with weak cough and aspiration of thin fluids from glottic incompetence.
steps.say: Superior nerve injury removes high pitch with early voice fatigue in singers noticeably. Supraglottic sensory loss creates silent aspiration risk after such injury. Recurrent injury gives breathy hoarseness with weak cough instead.

steps.tx: The **glottis**, the space between the true vocal folds including the rima glottidis, is the narrowest segment of the adult larynx and the level that decides voice and airway calibre together. Tumours here hoarsen early and spread late because lymphatics are sparse, the reverse of supraglottic behaviour. Subglottic narrowing, by contrast, threatens airway early while voice stays normal until late, inverting the symptom order.
steps.say: The space between true folds is the narrowest adult segment and decides voice quality. Sparse lymphatics delay spread and hoarseness gives early presentation here. Subglottic narrowing threatens airway while voice remains normal initially.

vis.alt: Laryngeal framework diagram with vocal folds, glottis and nerve supply shown.
vis.caption: Glottis and laryngeal nerve supply. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Reinke space** is the loose superficial lamina propria layer over the vocal fold that accumulates oedema in smokers, producing fusiform polypoid swelling and deep rough hoarseness. Its looseness allows the mucosal wave that endoscopic stroboscopy assesses for voice quality. Surgery that strips this layer scars the wave permanently, so voice surgery respects it as carefully as cancer surgery respects margins.
steps.say: Loose fold lining accumulates oedema in smokers and deepens voice quality noticeably. Mucosal wave movement across this layer indicates healthy voice production. Stripping injury scars the wave and needs careful avoidance.

steps.tx: The **pre-epiglottic space** in front of the epiglottis and the paraglottic space beside the ventricle are the deep highways by which supraglottic and glottic cancers spread silently beyond mucosal view. Imaging, not endoscopy alone, stages these spaces before larynx preservation is offered. Transglottic tumours crossing the ventricle occupy all three levels and historically required total laryngectomy more often than single level disease.
steps.say: Deep spaces around the epiglottis give cancer a silent route beyond mucosal view. Imaging stages these spaces before preservation treatment is offered safely. Tumours crossing all levels historically required total removal.

steps.tx: **Laryngeal lymphatics** divide sharply by level: supraglottis drains richly to upper and middle jugular nodes bilaterally, subglottis drains to prelaryngeal and paratracheal nodes, and glottis drains minimally. This anatomy explains early bilateral neck treatment for supraglottic cancer and observation of the neck in early glottic cancer. Delphian prelaryngeal node involvement warns of subglottic and thyroid extension in anterior tumours.
steps.say: Supraglottic drainage is rich and bilateral while glottic drainage is minimal comparatively. Neck treatment follows drainage anatomy by level in cancer planning. Prelaryngeal node involvement indicates anterior deep extension.

steps.tx: **Phonation** follows the myoelastic aerodynamic theory: expired air builds subglottic pressure until folds blow apart, elasticity and Bernoulli effect snap them shut, and the cycle repeats as audible vibration. Pitch rises with fold tension and length, loudness with subglottic pressure. Every voice therapy and surgery decision maps back to this cycle, because stiffness, gap and asymmetry each disturb a different phase of fold closure.
steps.say: Air pressure blows folds apart while elasticity snaps them shut in repeated vibration cycles. Tension controls pitch while pressure controls loudness in voice production. Stiffness, gap and asymmetry affect different closure phases distinctly.

right.title: Disordered phonation
points: Stiff wave from scar or oedema

steps.tx: The **myoelastic theory** completes the physiology examiners pair with nerve anatomy: muscles set fold position and tension, air supplies energy, tissue elasticity restores closure, and no neural impulse fires per vibration cycle. Lesions are therefore described mechanically as mass, stiffness or gap problems before treatment is chosen. A singer with pitch loss needs cricothyroid assessment, while a breathy patient needs closure assessment, and the theory tells you which to examine first.
steps.say: Muscles set tension while air supplies energy and elasticity restores closure cyclically. Neural impulses position folds without firing for every vibration cycle. Pitch loss needs tensor assessment while breathiness needs closure assessment.

cards.b: Posterior cricoarytenoid, supplied by recurrent laryngeal nerve; bilateral failure obstructs the airway.
External branch of superior laryngeal nerve; injury loses high pitch and causes vocal fatigue.
Sparse drainage, late nodes, early hoarseness; supraglottis drains richly and bilaterally.

keys: Posterior cricoarytenoid is the only cord abductor
All intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid use the recurrent nerve
Supraglottic cancer needs bilateral neck treatment
